maintopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-SUSPENSION OF SHARE LIMITATION

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-SUSPENSION OF SHARE LIMITATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to a question regarding the Bank of Western Canada that the Leader of the Opposition addressed on Tuesday to the President of the Treasury Board.
The charter of that bank, granted by this parliament, contains provisions that in most respects are similar to clauses 52 to 57 of the bill to revise the Bank Act that is now being studied in the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. It provides for a limit of 10 per cent in the number of shares of the bank that a shareholder and his associates may own, subject to a provision that the bank may accept subscriptions for shares by residents without regard to this limit, but no such subscriptions may be accepted by the bank except in accordance with and subject to such terms and conditions as the Treasury Board may by order prescribe.
When the promoters of this bank appeared before the standing committee they disclosed the number of shares for which the associated group of shareholders proposed to subscribe and the relationship among the various corporations making up the group. This information appears in the minutes of the committee. The proposed shareholdings were again disclosed to the board in the request by the bank to accept subscriptions from this group in excess of the 10 per cent limit that would otherwise apply.
The terms and conditions contained in order 658,534 are, I consider, quite appropriate to deal with the situation in which the
founding shareholders propose to have a majority interest during the early stages of the operations of the bank. These include a requirement that all shares of the bank in excess of the 10 per cent of the total outstanding that are held by the associated group must be disposed of before January 1, 1977, unless an extension is granted by the governor in council.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The proposed shareholdings of the associated group are listed in the treasury board order, the contents of which were made public by the Bank of Western Canada and which I would be very pleased to table if it is the wish of the house. I understand that because of a reorganization there have been some changes of ownership within the associated group but no increase in the total shares to be owned by all members of the group as stated in the order.
I have the treasury board minute and if the house so desires I would be very happy to table copies in both English and French.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-SUSPENSION OF SHARE LIMITATION
speechtext: Is it agreeable to the house that the minister table the treasury board minute to which he has referred?

maintopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-SUSPENSION OF SHARE LIMITATION
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-SUSPENSION OF SHARE LIMITATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter the minister has raised has given me some concern after reading about it in the newspapers and after being made aware of it as a result of the hearings before the committee to which the minister referred. I am somewhat disturbed by the implication in the minister's statement today that in the future this date of 1977 may possibly be extended still further. I am disturbed about it not only because it is in contravention of the act we now are in the process of passing through the committee but also because it lends further substance to the suspicions of the people of western Canada that this is not really a Bank of Western Canada because these institutions are based in the province of Ontario. I should like some assurance that the government would not permit this shareholding situation to continue beyond 1977, which seems to be generous in the extreme.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-SUSPENSION OF SHARE LIMITATION

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-231, to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions-Mr. Pickersgill-Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
When the committee rose last evening we were discussing new section 329 of clause 50 of the bill, with an amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. The amendment is as follows:
That clause 50 be amended by striking out section 329 on pages 41 and 42.
Is the committee ready for the question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Last evening I was saying a few words in support of the amendment. I should like to continue by summarizing as briefly as I can my reasons for thinking it would be detrimental to the position of western farmers if these rates were once again aired.
It appears obvious to me that the minister has gone to great lengths to make a deal with the railways. He has made an arrangement

January 18, 1967
Transportation
with the railways in which he has offered to give them something and they have offered to give him something in return. They are giving him very little, but under this particular clause we stand to give the railways a great deal. I should like to read what the minister said on this point to show how I reached the conclusion that he has made a deal, particularly with the C.P.R. As reported at page 11601 of Hansard, about half way down the right hand column, the minister said this, talking about the tax immunity granted to the C.P.R.:
We did make representations to them that this kind of immunity, which had been given in perpetuity, was not really the kind of thing that was very desirable in the twentieth century. The company did say that if they were allowed the kind of scope the government had said they were going to propose to parliament to enable the company to increase railway revenues, then tlm company would be glad to give up this immunity.
I should like to underline what was being said here. In essence the railway company pointed out that if they were allowed the kind of scope which the government had said it intended to propose to parliament, then the C.P.R. would be prepared to pay taxes on all their land across the prairies including, in particular, a number of cities in western Canada. This very paragraph outlines beyond a shadow of doubt that the hon. gentleman has been making arrangements with the C.P.R. in particular; and as Minister of Transport he would have included the C.N.R. in his arrangements.
I wish to read his words once more in order to make it clear that we have evidence that there was a deal, and that this particular clause was part of the deal. Under this clause we could lose more than is evident today, depending on the finding of the inquiry, and on the extent to which public opinion was aroused. The minister said-and I think this is worth reading again-
The company did say that if they were allowed the kind of scope the government had said they were going to propose to parliament to enable the company to increase railways revenues-
This would allow the company to pay taxes on all their property, particularly property in some of the western cities. Let me point out that this would amount to something like a million dollars a year in respect of each city out there.
So here is evidence that there was an arrangement, or a deal, made. I like the word "deal" because it suggests to a westerner that deals are sometimes shady. This deal could well be shady if the results of this inquiry 
come out on the wrong side of the ledger as far as the Crowsnest pass rates are concerned. That is the shady part of it, and I do not like it. I believe it would be much better if this section were to come out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman has left that subject, would he permit me to say a word about it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I should like to continue. I want to see this transportation bill through as quickly as I can.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I know the hon. gentleman does not wish to misrepresent anything. I would just like to say that the statement of mine which he quoted had reference to the public statements which had been made. It had no reference to anything privately said to any railway company but to the public statement to the effect that we intended to introduce legislation to free the railway rates and permit competition. It had no relation whatsoever, in any shape or form, to the Crowsnest pass rates.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: It is all very well for the minister to say that. That is why I prefer to call it a shady deal, because we do not know. Let us strike out this clause.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman; the hon. gentleman and I have had amicable relations so far and I know he does not want to destroy them by questioning my word with regard to something I said myself. I am confident that the hon. member believes that the statement I have just made to the committee is a truthful statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I am not doubting the minister's word. I am drawing attention to the provision which is included in this bill, the bill now before us. Whether he intended it to be in the bill does not matter. I do not think he did, because he says he did not. But it is in the bill now, and we do not like it. We do not like this section because it now becomes part and parcel of the arrangement the minister made, and it may be detrimental to the western farmer in the years ahead, particularly if public opinion can be aroused against these rates which were set so long ago.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Subsection 1 of the new section reads in part:
-at the level of rates referred to in subsection (2) and shall report such revenues and costs to
January 18, 1967

the governor in council and the amount of payments necessary, in the opinion of the commission, to assist such railway companies to meet the costs of operations-
Is this concerned with allowing the farmers to get their products to market and affording them equal opportunity to market their products? There is no mention of that, but that is what the Crowsnest Pass rates were intended to do in conjunction with the quota system.
This new section is concerned with the railway companies and that is why I think it was placed in the bill as part and parcel of the arrangement that was made. Some hon. members opposite may wonder why I get a little worked up over something like this, but the Crowsnest pass rates are the Magna Carta of western Canada. We see the thin edge of the wedge in this new section and this is why we are making a determined stand to try to convince the minister that it should be deleted.
I would be the first to say that the minister has really tried to be co-operative, and by this amendment we are urging him to be more co-operative. We will not mind if ten years from now the government and the minister, if he is still Minister of Transport, say: Let us have a review of the Crowsnest pass rates. By that time railway equipment may be modernized and there might be a possibility that the rates might be reduced.
The new section provides that a study of the rates must be completed within three years. What is the use of a three year study when we have just received the MacPherson commission report and that commission could not come to a conclusion on cost figures? As I mentioned in an earlier speech, a start has just been made on the modernization of the railways' grain movement plant. That modernization is only in the embryonic stage. Elevator companies are suddenly becoming concerned about the fact that they will have to build bigger elevators, and the railway companies are concerned about their outdated handling equipment.
As recorded at page 13 of the proceedings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines of 1964-65, the former president of the C.N.R., Donald Gordon, said:
Yet, despite the fact that there have been many radical and fundamental changes in western Canada's economy since those explosive years, the system of grain handling established before the first world war-the collection, storage and transport of the prairie grain crop-has changed very little.
He went on to day:
Many of the existing country elevators are now well below the optimum size for the best economic
Transportation
costs of operation and also for the most economic
cost of trans-shipment by railways..The second
factor involves the economies that can be obtained through a program of elevator consolidation that would eliminate those existing elevators that are operating well below the size required to ensure lowest cost operation.
The proposed three year study will not be able to take into account the fact that the railways' equipment is outdated.
Because the Crowsnest pass rates were first established in 1898 and reaffirmed in 1925 there is a good deal of feeling across the country that they are outdated and must be increased. But as I pointed out previously, the cost of moving a cubic yard of dirt has not gone up because of automation. New, huge equipment has made the moving of earth more economic than by the old horse and slip method. Slow progress has been made in modernizing grain transport equipment, and if it were modernized possibly the rates could be lowered. But such prejudice has been generated against the rates that I believe it would be difficult to place any group of men on the board of review who had not already formed an opinion about them. How could such a group judge the rates if they have already subconsciously prejudged them?
From private conversations with members of the government I know that many of them have said, "You know very well that the rates are outdated and must be raised." I say they have formed opinions without any real study of the problem, and the general feeling is that the rates must be raised.
The Minister of Transport has guaranteed that as long as he occupies that position the rates will not be touched in any way. But that is no real guarantee. His parliamentary secretary, who may have aspirations to become minister of transport, gave plenty of evidence at three or four committee meetings of his feeling that the rates are outdated and should be raised. How do we know he will not be the next minister of transport? Someone says that is doubtful. For myself I say I hope he is not.
My sixth point is that the Crowsnest pass rates could provide a sizeable profit for the railroads if it were not for the quota system, but that has become part and parcel of the rates and should be maintained. The rates and the quota system are essential to give farmers equal rights to market their products.
Let us look briefly at the question of whether or not the railways are losing money. Before the freeze was placed on railway freight rates, which situation will continue to apply until this bill is passed, if railways wanted to
1IS54

January 18, 1967
Transportation
increase freight rates they had to apply to the Board of Transport Commissioners for permission. They had to prove that they were losing money, that they were not getting a proper return on their investment, and if they did that they could then apply a horizontal freight rate increase. I may have given an abbreviated description of the process, but that is what railways had to do when they wished to increase freight rates.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Let us look at the question and go back to the year 1957. The railways said they were losing money in the movement of grain. In 1958 a freeze on freight rates was imposed. In 1957 and 1958 the railways said that they were using the profits made in the movement of other goods to cover the losses sustained in the movement of grain. The freeze on freight rates has continued since that time and the railways have not been able to increase them. The movement of grain has doubled, freight rates have been frozen, but what has hap-ened? Railway profits have continued to rise. Even the C.N.R., which has a huge debt hanging over its head on which it has to pay interest, has been able to widen the difference between their operating costs and their total revenue. How can they come before parliament and say that this new section is necessary and that we should re-examine this aspect?
Another objection I have to this provision is that it states that the commission shall inquire into the revenues and costs. Then farther along in the subsection we see the words "and shall report such revenues and costs to the governor in council". There is no mention, as was the case in respect of Bill C-120, of what these costs are. Are these costs to be compensatory costs or the total cost which takes in all the fixed costs? There is no mention of this in the subsection.
In other words, if the commissioners saw fit to do so they could represent to the governor in council that the railways needed a marginal mark-up of another 30 per cent to cover the total of fixed and variable costs. Anyone who understands the principle of volume hauling understands that the greater the volume the less the charge for fixed costs. There is no mention of this in this section, but in the old bill there was mention of variable costs plus a $9 million expenditure toward fixed costs.
I have another point to make in respect of my request that this section be deleted. Who is going to speak? The railways will present

their facts to the board of review and the board will have to judge whether or not their costs have been met and how much the subsidy should be. The board will have to decide how much it should allow for fixed costs and how much it should allow for variable costs. Who will present the other side of the argument? In any court case both sides of the argument are heard. Who is going to rise and speak for the prairie farmers? The minister might say that the pools, the provincial governments or any other interested party will. But is that enough? An interested party may not feel that it is his responsibility to spend $1J million. This is the amount the Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan governments spent in respect of the MacPherson commission.
Are we going to expect the Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan governments to spend another $1J million and again bring in from the United States experts such as Mr. Borts and Mr. Williams? These two experts have already presented a brief but I imagine they would be prepared to do a costing study again if the provincial governments wished to hire them. This government is putting the prairie provinces immediately on the defensive. That is the reason I urge the minister to reconsider the decision he made last night that this section shall remain and that we shall vote on it. I urge the minister to wipe it out. Already the minister has been successful in taking our suggestions and having them redrafted. Let us change this three-year period to ten years. Let us include in the bill a phrase to the effect that the Crowsnest pass rates will extend until 1975.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Order. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at length because I am going to try to accept the excellent advice given me more than once by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. There are, however, a couple of specific questions raised by the hon. gentleman which I really ought to answer before a vote is taken, if it is the intention that there should be a vote on this clause. The first question the hon. gentleman asked concerned what guarantee there is that the Crowsnest pass rates will continue. He said he believed that as long as I was the Minister of Transport they were quite safe. I thank him for that expression of confidence. But these rates are in the law; they cannot be changed unless a majority of members of parliament
January 18, 1967



are convinced that the law should be changed. That is the guarantee. Surely that is much better than a guarantee from me. I can also assure the hon. gentleman that my parliamentary secretary is more likely to go to the other place before I do, so I do not think he need worry about that particular problem.
In respect of the review I should like to say that the review is not of the rates. There is to be no review of the rates. If there should be a suggestion that there be a review of the rates 1 would vote against any such proposal. There is to be no review whatsoever of the rates; they are guaranteed in the present law and they are guaranteed in this bill. All that is to be reviewed is the cost in respect of carrying the grain. The reason this is in the bill, instead of the provision to pay the railways which was in Bill C-120, is that I am not convinced the railways should get anything. I am not convinced the railways are not making money from carrying grain. Therefore I would not put anything in this bill which in effect would ask parliament to pay them anything. All I have said is that we want to get the facts, that we should not pay them anything for three years. At the end of the three years, if the facts show that there is a loss then all this section says is that the commission should report to the governor in council and recommend that he take such action as he may see fit to take. It does not say that the loss shall be paid.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: In the review it would be difficult to determine the accuracy of fixed costs. You cannot ascertain properly whether grain is being carried at too low or too high a rate. Is not the weakness of the review the fact that you cannot really review anything. The railways-and I have appeared before boards-always say that fixed costs are allocated.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
As a matter of fact the railways will not do that; the commission will do it. The commission will be appointed by the government. There is also the implication that the governor in council would ask parliament to make good the loss. Therefore the Minister of Finance will be a party on the other side. The farmers will not have to do this because the farmers rights are guaranteed in the bill. The person who will have an
Transportation
interest on the other side will be the Minister of Finance, and the commission will know that. They will know, if they find there are losses, that there will be an implication that these losses should be met out of the treasury.
Any government with any sense of responsibility will see to it that every submission made by the railways to this commission is subject to the utmost scrutiny. No minister of finance likes to pay subsidies to the railways or anybody else and then have to make himself and his government unpopular by imposing taxes. This, I think, is the real basis of the thing.
The hon. member asked who would speak on the other side. I say that it will be the Minister of Finance; it will also be the Minister of Transport. He is not the agent of the railways; he is the agent of the people of Canada. It is his duty and it is the duty of the Minister of Finance to protect the treasury. No government, with so many other ways of spending the taxpayers' money, will want to pay a nickel in subsidies to the railways unless they are thoroughly justified.
This bill gives a better guaranty to the farmers if section 329 is left in than if it is left out. With this section in the bill there is no reason for anybody to agitate to change the Crowsnest rates.
The railways will know that after three years the facts will be reviewed by somebody who is impartial, and if there is in fact a loss it would seem reasonable justice that it be made up. The railways therefore will have no motive to agitate to have the rates changed. If we have no provision for such a review, if we say we do not think it is necessary to have it, I suggest that the railway companies would, and probably quite justifiably, continue agitation. The fear that because this review will take place there will be agitation-and this is my opinion-is misplaced. If we had no review I think the railways would constantly agitate to have such a review. But if they know it will be held and if they know that this law safeguards these rights, as I have said a dozen times I do not think that any government I can foresee, not even-

speechtext: Be careful.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: -an N.D.P. government, in the unlikely event that we have one, would touch the Crowsnest rates.

What about the hon. member for Lapointe?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I agree completely with the view that these rates are there and they are there to stay. The whole philosophy of the bill is that if in the national interest we ask the railways to perform certain functions they are entitled to perform those at a compensatory level. If we say they must do so at a level that is not compensatory, but it is still in the public interest to have it done, the railways should receive reasonable compensation for it. This does not provide compulsory compensation. They can come back to parliament-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Would the hon. minister permit a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Does the minister not concede that even if this section were not in the bill the commission could make a study of the economic aspects of the Crowsnest rates under clause 15, which has already been passed?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: It would not be the same kind of review. If the hon. gentleman looks at clause 15 and the provisions set forth there, he will see it deals primarily with research.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: This section singles out the farmer. The government is singling out the farmer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Perhaps I should say a word about that. It does single out the farmers. It says that the wheat farmer alone, or almost alone, of all the shippers in Canada shall have a fixed rate. In practically all other instances, though there are a few which have been temporarily frozen for one or two years, the railways may change rates so long as they have them high enough to be compensatory and below a certain maximum established to protect the public. We are saying that the grain farmers-and this includes more than wheat because all grains are specified here-alone are guaranteed a fixed rate that will not be changed. In that sense they are singled out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Would the minister permit another question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Perhaps when I have
finished. We are saying that if it is proven that because of that fixed rate there is a loss it will be competent to ask parliament to make up that loss. It is not as though we are leaving it up to the railways; the railways would have to earn the loss or make it good somewhere else. The view that Mr. MacPherson took, and

I share it with him, is that other freight shippers should not be expected to bear the losses in carrying freight for just some shippers. This subject was well covered in an editorial in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of August 31 last year in these words:
A national transport regulatory agency can be a good thing-if it doesn't set up a stifling red-tape bureaucracy .... A national transportation policy based solely on "compensatory" freight rates (i.e., keeping only profitable lines operating) could do immense harm to the maritimes. So far, Ottawa seems to be keeping this in mind. It will be up to the Atlantic provinces to be sure their interests are protected as parliament legislates in this crucial field.

I should also like to quote a report which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle Herald of December 6 last year of an address by J. W. E. Mingo, chairman of the Halifax port commission, to an Atlantic ports day conference. Mr. Mingo said there were approximately 24 months left before the new legislation would affect the maritimes. He counselled his audience to "use this time wisely" in an effort to ensure that the final bill will contain statutory guarantees to protect "the captive shipper" from crippling freight rates.
He went on to point out, as I have already stated, that rates are governed at present by the Maritime Freight Rates Act and said that the assistance provided by it is designed to place eastern manufacturers and shippers on a price parity basis with their central Canadian competitors. In order to deal at all adequately with the subject matter of the amendment I think I should make two observations. In all the observations made so far with regard to proposed new section 335 I think there has perhaps been a confusion of two things. So far as the Maritime Freight Rates Act is concerned, this bill touches it in no way whatsoever. That act is in exactly the force and effect in which it has been since the amendments were made pursuant to the recommendations of Mr. Walter Harris in his budget in 1957.
What this clause does is carry on the freeze of the railway rates themselves, which freeze has been in force since 1959. That freeze is going to be lifted everywhere west of Levis, but in the select territory this bill provides that it shall continue for two more years certain. Of course, parliament in its wisdom could extend that period or abridge it if it wanted to do so. If we decided to make some fundamental changes which made the freeze no longer appropraite, this could be done by a future parliament. In other words, we are saying that unless some express change is made so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned, that is, in the select territory, there will be no change at all in the present situation as a result of this bill, with one relatively minor exception.
In other words, we are saying that because this study is going on, because it is nearly completed, and because in my view we want to stimulate the government, it is better to have this freeze for two years than to have the nagging stimulus that would prevail if the freeze were not in effect. I would be very

Transportation
much afraid, considering that the freeze was put on in 1959 and is still in effect in 1967, that if we did not have any limit on it there might be a disposition to leave the problem dormant and not get on with the job.
We could have done it either way. That is precisely the reason I decided to recommend to parliament that there should be this change. The only respect in which the rates in the maritime provinces in the select territory will be changed at all is that the freeze will not apply to less than carload lots. As hon. members know, the railways are amalgamating express and less than carload lot freight. After the most anxious consideration, the standing committee decided to recommend to the house that we remove the freeze on the freight part of that system. It seemed on balance that this was the best thing to do, and I admit that it was a fine balance. Some of the rates will go up, others will go down. Express rates will go down quite markedly and they will now, of course, come under the general regulatory powers of this legislation.
I came to the conclusion, after examining the best evidence I could obtain, that on balance we would get a better rate structure, more efficiency and more zeal on the part of the railways to handle this traffic well if they were freed than would otherwise be the case. I say this out of a rather long experience of spending my summers in Newfoundland waiting, waiting and waiting for things to arrive. If we can get a real express system for less than carload lots, it will be of far more use to the Atlantic region than freezing some rates that create a disincentive on the part of the railway to move the traffic fast. There are all kinds of people today who ship by air freight to the Atlantic provinces and pay three or four times as much because that is the one way to assure speedy delivery. I am dwelling on this point, Mr. Chairman, because I would not want any hon. member to say I had deceived the committee by leaving it out.
However, this provision for a freeze is there for two years unless parliament decides to do something different. I would hope we would just leave it that way. The people who are doing this study have been asked to advise the government upon what measures should be taken to improve the whole of transportation within the Atlantic provinces. The reason for this freeze is to keep the present situation unchanged until there is time for the government to recommend to parliament positive steps to improve the situation in the Atlantic provinces. These positive steps might conceivably involve other things. I hope they will not be limited to the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I hope they will not be limited to the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Perhaps I should not detail my hopes because I might be sticking my neck out. I think all hon. members from that part of the country know that I feel it is not just in the field of railways that we need improvement in transportation in the Atlantic region. It seems to me that if there is a deadline here any government that is in office is not going to want to lose its support in that region, if I may put it at its lowest terms. If it were continued indefinitely there might be a tendency to say, well, other pieces of legislation affecting other parts of the country are more urgent, there is more pressure, so we can roll this over for another year.
